title: Do Deterministic Verifiers Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Paired Shared‑Candidate Evaluation
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired experiment (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that measured whether coupling a deterministic NetOps verifier+gate (generate→validate→repair, max 1 automated repair) to a single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini) changes safety outcomes when the identical initial LLM candidate is observed with and without gating. Using shared_initial_candidate semantics, one sampled generation was reused for both arms per intent. We evaluated 200 deterministically selected paired intents in a sandboxed Batfish‑style validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). All 200 shared initial candidates passed validation in both baseline and guarded arms (contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered paired estimand (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired‑bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No automated repairs were applied. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory contrast tests only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates; it does not measure guarded‑conditioned regeneration, prompt engineering, or multi‑sample/model variance. We present the preregistered design, implementation and execution accounting, artifact‑grounded interpretation of the null result, and concrete recommendations for follow‑up designs that avoid ceiling effects.

sections.introduction:
Generative language models are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level operator intent into device configurations and maintenance workflows for network operations (NetOps). Deploying such capabilities in production requires evidence that model outputs do not introduce reachability, isolation, or policy violations when applied to real networks. Prior surveys and empirical reports emphasize that operational trustworthiness depends strongly on the surrounding system machinery—retrieval, deterministic validators, gates, and repair loops—rather than on the model alone [1]–[3]. Architectures that combine generation with deterministic validation and bounded repair (generate→validate→repair) are widely advocated, but reproducible paired evidence that isolates the verifier/gate effect on identical model candidates is limited [3],[4].

Research question. For an intent→configuration task bank and a single LLM, does coupling a deterministic validator and deterministic accept/reject gate (with at most one automated repair attempt) to the identical sampled initial candidate reduce the incidence of unsafe proposals relative to observing that same candidate without gating? We formalized this as the preregistered estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered paired design and frozen execution (autocand_A1_prereg_v1) that fixed generation semantics, sampling, model, validator, gating policy, and analysis prior to observation; (2) an autonomous confirmatory run using gpt‑5‑mini and a Batfish‑style deterministic validator on n=200 deterministically selected paired intents with shared_initial_candidate semantics; (3) artifact‑grounded analysis showing complete concordance (all candidates valid) and no repair activity; (4) an interpretation of ceiling effects grounded in archived artifacts; and (5) concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for follow‑up preregistered designs that permit nondegenerate inference of verifier/gate value.
sections.related_work:
LLM‑assisted NetOps and AIOps research covers intent‑based configuration translation, runbook generation, log/RCA, and early agentic automation proposals. Surveys and empirical studies document hallucination and unsafe command risks in operational contexts and argue for validator‑coupled pipelines, RAG anchoring, and external safety checks [1],[2],[5].

Generate→validate→repair approaches appear across domains. In program repair and related software‑engineering applications, LLM‑based generate‑and‑validate systems have produced empirical improvements under specific datasets and validator designs; neural verification and distribution‑modeling work also proposes and evaluates external checking as a safety path [6],[7]. These cited records support the proposition that external deterministic checks plus repair loops can improve outputs in particular controlled settings, but each report is task‑ and validator‑specific; none implies universal safety guarantees for NetOps. This motivates a paired experimental design that isolates the validator/gate effect on identical first‑pass generations while preserving preregistered semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and frozen plan. We preregistered study autocand_A1_prereg_v1 before any model calls. The preregistration fixed the primary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline), generation semantics = shared_initial_candidate, model/adaptor (gpt‑5‑mini via hosted_netops_gvr_v1), deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and gate policy, repair budget (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1), task selection rule and sample size (task_count = 200 paired intents), and the confirmatory analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1). These items and parameter values were frozen and archived prior to observing outputs; preregistration SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest.

Generation semantics and sampling. The execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent exactly one initial LLM generation was produced and deterministically reused by both baseline and guarded arms. Under this semantics the confirmatory estimand evaluates only validator/repair/gate effects on the same initial candidate; it does not measure any effect of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model sampling variance. Task selection followed the adapter's deterministic index rule to produce a fixed, outcome‑independent sample of 200 paired intents from a synthetic generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). Per‑task difficulty labels (e.g., "very_hard" and "extreme") are part of the archived task manifest.

Models, adapter, validator, and configuration. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json records declared_model_version="gpt-5-mini" and provider="openai_responses"). Adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementing Batfish‑style checks (sequence ordering, interface precondition checks, final_group and minimum_up constraints, protected interfaces, and reachability/policy consistency). The recorded model configuration included max_output_tokens=2000, maximum_attempts_per_call=1, reasoning_effort="minimal", and temperature=null. We emphasize that a null/unset temperature value is not evidence of deterministic sampling; the adapter produced a single sampled generation per pair which was then reused (shared_initial_candidate). No claim of deterministic model sampling is made.

Interventions, gating, and scoring. Baseline: observe the shared initial candidate without gating. Guarded: feed the identical shared initial candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5; the deterministic gate applied a preregistered accept/reject rule and, upon violations, allowed up to one automated repair attempt. Primary outcome: binary unsafe_flag = any reachability or workflow/policy violation reported by the validator after candidate stabilization. Scoring used the rule full_intent_constraint_validation; per‑episode validator traces and repair flags were archived.

Confirmatory analysis. The primary confirmatory analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1. The paired 2×2 contingency compares unsafe_flag between baseline and guarded across pairs; exact two‑sided testing (McNemar‑equivalent) and a paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000) were preregistered. Missingness policy (complete_pair_primary) and a single retry rule for infra errors were preregistered.

Implementation and archival hygiene. Model-provider traces, shared_initial generations, per‑episode responses, validator traces, repair traces, task manifest, and analysis outputs were recorded contemporaneously and archived under the execution bundle. The execution manifest contains checksumming and reconciliation metadata to support byte‑level verification.
sections.results:
Execution summary and accounting. The run executed as preregistered: start 2026‑08‑31T13:49:34Z, complete 2026‑08‑31T14:14:32Z. Planned_episode_count = 400 (200 pairs), completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0. Model calls used = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair) as recorded in the provider audit; no retries were required.

Primary confirmatory outcome. The paired contingency of guarded × baseline is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (all shared initial candidates were scored VALID_CONFIGURATION by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in both arms). The paired estimate (guarded minus baseline unsafe‑proposal rate) = 0.0; exact two‑sided p = 1.0. The paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI is [0.0,0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). The zero‑width CI and p = 1.0 follow directly from the absence of discordant pairs under the registered estimand and the archived analysis outputs.

Repair activity and diagnostics. repair_applied = false for every guarded episode; repair_provider_trace_path fields are null in scoring artifacts. Representative episodes (e.g., task‑000004) show parsed_command_count == required_command_count and validator validation_after.valid = true. The task bank exercised common workflow constraints (VLAN migration, uplink failover, MTU change, redundancy group invariants) and the validator checked sequencing and preconditions per task payloads.

Missingness, contamination and reconciliation. Missingness_summary reports complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed/unscorable episodes. Contamination checks flagged no items. Deterministic reconciliation asserts consistent episode accounting and that all deterministic consistency checks passed. These artifacts support the quantitative outcomes reported above.

Latency notes. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics required a single model call per pair, model_call accounting equals 200. The guarded arm incurred validator evaluation time but no automated repairs; per‑pair wall time was dominated by deterministic validator execution. Exact latency distributions are archived in the execution logs for reproducibility.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded interpretation. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the confirmatory estimand isolates only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates. Observing n11 = 200 implies that, for the chosen model (gpt‑5‑mini), the selected synthetic task bank, the prompt/template family, and the validator ruleset, the sampled initial candidates satisfied the validator constraints so the guarded machinery applied no repairs and changed no acceptance decisions. The execution and analysis artifacts support this conclusion directly.

Why the CI is degenerate. The paired bootstrap CI is degenerate because no discordant pairs exist; every bootstrap resample of paired outcomes yields paired difference 0.0 producing zero empirical variance and CI [0.0,0.0]. This is an expected inferential outcome, not an analysis error.

Ceiling‑effect contributors. The archived artifacts indicate three contributors: (1) task‑bank alignment—the synthetic generator encoded required_sequences and workflow_policies closely matching prompt expectations, increasing the probability of syntactically correct model outputs; (2) validator tightness—the validator encoded the same sequencing and precondition checks used during task synthesis so correct mappings passed validation readily; and (3) shared_initial_candidate semantics prevented any guarded‑conditioned regeneration or model variance that might produce discordant outcomes. Each contributor is traceable in the archived task manifest, scoring traces, and model configuration.

Design implications and recommendations. To permit nondegenerate measurement of verifier/gate value we recommend (artifact‑supported): (a) augmenting the task bank with adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents to raise baseline unsafe rates (the archived generator exposes generation_seed and difficulty metadata that can be adjusted); (b) running an alternative confirmatory design that uses independent generation per condition (two independent model calls per pair) to capture guarded‑conditioned regeneration and model sampling variance (this increases model_call budget predictably); (c) testing multiple model variants or sampling temperatures to expose model variance effects (execution/model_configuration.json records model and temperature fields for modification); (d) increasing automated repair budget or enabling iterative repair loops to evaluate repair effectiveness when initial violations are present; and (e) including human‑in‑the‑loop arms to assess operator responses to validator flags. These recommendations follow directly from the artifact evidence and the statistical meaning of the shared_initial_candidate estimand.

Scope and caveats. The null result is specific to the chosen experimental regime (single LLM, synthetic task bank, deterministic selection, validator ruleset, shared_initial_candidate semantics) and does not contradict prior evidence that validators can reduce unsafe outputs under different regimes (e.g., independent per‑condition generation, adversarial items, multiple samples) [1]–[3],[6]. Operational deployment requires broader evaluations including adversarial tests, multiple models, HITL assessments, and live‑device safety checks.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired experiment comparing an LLM‑alone observation to the same initial candidate after deterministic verification and bounded automated repair. Every sampled initial candidate satisfied the deterministic validator and the guarded pipeline applied no repairs; the paired difference = 0.0 (p = 1.0) with paired‑bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0,0.0]. This null result demonstrates how preregistered generation semantics, task design, and validator alignment can produce ceiling effects that nullify a paired shared‑candidate contrast. We archive full artifacts and recommend follow‑up preregistered designs that intentionally increase baseline unsafe rates or permit independent per‑condition generation to quantify verifier/gate contributions under more challenging conditions. All core artifacts and analysis outputs supporting these conclusions are archived in the execution bundle.

disclosure_statement: Preregistration and autonomy: this study was preregistered as autocand_A1_prereg_v1 and executed autonomously after the autonomy lock. Models and tools: single LLM = gpt‑5‑mini (provider recorded as openai_responses); orchestration/adapter = hosted_netops_gvr_v1; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5; task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. Human role and autonomy boundary: the human Research Director selected the topical family and constrained the initial prompt pre‑lock; literature review, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer‑review emulation, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock; no human manually edited manuscript technical content after the lock. Generation semantics clarification: the executed and preregistered generation semantics were shared_initial_candidate (one initial sampled generation reused by both arms per pair); therefore the confirmatory estimand measures only validator/repair/gate effects on identical first‑pass candidates rather than effects from guarded‑conditioned regeneration or multiple independent model samples. limitations: Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics mean baseline and guarded conditions began from an identical initial candidate; the confirmatory estimand therefore measures only validator/repair/gate effects on that same candidate and cannot assess effects of guarded‑conditioned regeneration or prompt engineering.

Construct validity: tasks were synthetic and deterministically selected; the binary unsafe_flag depends on validator coverage (reachability and workflow sequencing rules) and may not capture all operational risks (transient performance regressions, vendor‑specific side effects outside validator rules).

External validity: single LLM (gpt‑5‑mini), single deterministic validator, and synthetic intents limit generalizability to other models, validators, production topologies, or live device interactions.

Conclusion validity: the observed null effect (paired difference = 0) reflects this execution's sampling frame where baseline generation produced only valid candidates; the study was powered to detect ~10 percentage‑point reductions but cannot rule out smaller effects under different sampling or adversarial inputs.
Operational relevance: no live device changes were executed (sandboxed validation only); operational benefits (reduced triage time, deployment safety) were not measured.
Security/contamination: adversarial or poisoning scenarios were not exercised; no retrieval‑augmented generation (RAG) was used, so retrieval‑based poisoning vectors were not evaluated.

Task‑bank reporting: the archived task_manifest.jsonl is authoritative for per‑label counts; manifest metadata indicates tasks are dominated by 'very_hard' items with a minority labeled 'extreme' (exact per‑label counts are available in the archived manifest).
